normalized.governing_thought: Executive summary: raise prices in 2027, but target mid-market and enterprise and keep SMB prices flat until a test proves they can rise
executive_summary: Answer: yes, with a targeted increase. At 2027 renewals, raise mid-market +12% and enterprise up to its contract terms. Hold SMB prices, exempt the 2025 promotion cohort and test core SMB before raising it. The plan adds ≈$4.1M of net ARR (the CFO's $10.3M headline is ≈$5.0M once timing and churn are counted), keeps NRR above 100%, and leaves the 15% growth target needing only ≈$0.9M of new-customer ARR.

1. Churn is rising because of one cohort, not because customers are reacting to price. About 90% of the SMB churn rise (2.0% → 3.1% a month) comes from the 2,100 customers who joined on the 2025 half-price promotion. They churn at ≈4.9% a month. Churn among other SMB customers only moved from 2.0% to 2.1%, and the share of them citing price held at 18% (19% in 2025).

2. Pricing power sits in mid-market and enterprise, not SMB. Mid-market and enterprise are 76% of ARR, with 112–118% NRR and monthly churn of 0.8% or less. A +10% mid-market test showed no significant conversion loss, and Inkwell has not appeared in deals above 200 seats. In SMB, Inkwell sells a $9 plan and Palisade's win rate against it fell from 51% to 38%.

3. The CFO's $10.3M is really ≈$5.0M. The targeted plan keeps ≈$4.1M of that with less risk. Renewal timing and the 7% enterprise caps leave $7.6M that can be repriced in 2027, and expected churn cuts that to ≈$5.0M. Leaving SMB out costs ≈$1.0M in the base case. It raises the downside floor from $2.5M to $3.1M and avoids raising prices on customers who are already leaving over price.

4. Roll it out in stages, with guardrails. Reprice mid-market and enterprise renewals from January, and drop mid-market to +10% if Q1 churn goes above 1.0% a month. Run a randomised +8% test on core SMB in Q1 and extend it from May only if it passes. Exempt the promotion cohort and fund its onboarding. Reset the budget line and define the churn figure the board sees.

slides.title: We tested the CFO's plan first. It held for mid-market and enterprise but failed on SMB and on value, so we changed the answer

claims.claim: Initial hypothesis (CFO proposal): raise list prices 12% on every plan at renewal from January 2027, adding $10.3M of ARR.
1. Rising churn is not a reaction to price across the customer base — Holds, with a caveat: churn alone is no reason to freeze prices, but the promotion cohort must be exempt
evidence: About 90% of the SMB rise comes from the promotion cohort
Core SMB churn went 2.0% → 2.1% and its share citing price went 19% → 18%
the promotion cohort itself left over price: 52% cite it, and most left within two months of the discount ending

claims.claim: 2. Every segment can absorb +12% with little loss — Fails for SMB: raise mid-market and enterprise; hold SMB and test it
evidence: Mid-market: a +10% test showed no significant conversion loss, 112% NRR, no Inkwell above 200 seats
Enterprise: 118% NRR, 0.2% churn
SMB: $9 Inkwell plan, win rate 51% → 38%, uplift roughly break-even in the downside case

claims.claim: 3. The increase is worth ≈$10.3M in 2027 — Fails: budget ≈$4.1M, not $10.3M
evidence: Only $7.6M can be repriced in 2027: 15% of mid-market and 60% of enterprise ARR do not renew, and 7% caps apply
Expected churn takes it to ≈$5.0M

claims.claim: 4. The plan keeps NRR above 100% and supports 15% growth — Holds: the constraints don't stop it; the risk is in execution
evidence: NRR rises from 109% to ≈114% (≈113% in the downside case)
The 15% target then needs ≈$0.9M of new-customer ARR

claims.claim: Revised answer: raise prices where retention is strong (mid-market +12%, enterprise up to contract terms) and hold SMB, exempting the 2025 promotion cohort and testing core SMB before any increase.

slides.title: About 90% of the rise in SMB churn comes from the 2025 promotion cohort; churn among other SMB customers barely moved

claims.claim: About 90% of the rise in SMB churn comes from the 2025 promotion cohort; churn among other SMB customers barely moved
evidence: SMB monthly logo churn: H1 2025 2.0%, H1 2026 3.1%, +1.1pp
of which promotion cohort (2,100): n/a → ≈4.9%, new
Mid-market: 0.6% → 0.8%, +0.2pp
Enterprise: 0.2% → 0.2%, 0.0pp
Chart: SMB churn H1 2025 2.0%; drift in core +0.1pp; promotion cohort effect +1.0pp; SMB churn H1 2026 3.1%

Promotion cohort churn = (5,900 × 3.1% − 3,800 × 2.1%) ÷ 2,100 = 4.9% a month. Its effect = 2,100/5,900 × (4.9% − 2.1%) = 1.0pp, or 91% of the rise in churned customers. Uses mid-2026 customer counts for both halves.

claims.claim: The promotion cohort is 36% of SMB customers and 21% of SMB ARR ($4.4M), but supplies ≈103 of the ≈183 SMB customers lost each month (56%).
Exit surveys tell the same story: the 34% overall price share implies the cohort makes up ≈47% of churners. That is close to the 56% estimated above.
The rise is a one-off effect from one cohort. As the cohort shrinks, blended SMB churn should drift back towards ≈2.1%.
Mid-market churn also edged up, from 0.6% to 0.8%. The pack gives no cause, so we treat it as a watch item (page 15).

slides.title: Promotion customers leave for two reasons, weak activation and the discount ending, so onboarding alone won't fix it and a price rise would hit them hardest

claims.claim: Activation explains ≈30% of the cohort's extra churn
evidence: Only 41% of promotion customers sent 5+ documents in their first month, against 72% for other cohorts
Chart: core SMB churn 2.1%; weaker activation (41% vs 72%) +0.8pp; discount cliff and other +2.0pp; promotion cohort churn 4.9%

Activation effect: customers sending fewer than 5 documents in month 1 churn ≈3× as often. Core: 0.72c + 0.28×3c = 2.1% → c = 1.35%. Promotion cohort at 41% activated: 0.41c + 0.59×3c = 2.9%. The remaining 2.0pp is what activation doesn't explain.

claims.claim: This supports the Head of Customer Success: many never set the product up.
The discount ending explains most of the rest (≈70%)
evidence: 52% of promotion churners cite price, against 18% of core SMB churners
Most promotion customers who left did so within two months of the 50% discount ending, so they reacted to a doubling of what they paid

claims.claim: The CFO is right that core churn is not about price, but wrong that churn is only an onboarding problem. This cohort has just shown it is very sensitive to price.
Exempt it from any 2027 increase ($4.4M ARR, 2,100 customers) and target onboarding at the 59% who never activated.

alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: "Leaves proven pricing power unused"; $0 net ARR; needs $4.9M new-customer ARR for +15%.

alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: tested as the initial hypothesis; fails for SMB and on value ($10.3M is ≈$5.0M; $2.5M downside). "Highest base case, but the risk sits where churn is already rising"; exposes $21.0M SMB ARR incl. promotion cohort; SMB part −$0.6M in downside; ≈$0.4M ARR a year ongoing SMB churn drag from 2028.

alternatives_considered.option: C. Targeted increase (mid-market +12%, enterprise up to terms, SMB held and tested, promotion cohort exempt)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Chosen: "Best risk-adjusted value; recommended"; $4.1M ($3.1M downside), +$0.5M if SMB test passes.

alternatives_considered.option: Variant of C with mid-market at +10% (the tested level)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Nets $3.5M ($2.7M downside). "It is the fallback, not the default"; +12% nets ≈$0.5M more in both base and downside cases; used if Q1 mid-market churn exceeds 1.0% a month.

alternatives_considered.option: Treating churn as only an onboarding problem / onboarding halving SMB churn (Head of Customer Success claim)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected as a full explanation: activation explains ≈30% of the cohort's extra churn; 'halve churn' claim doesn't hold; plan on a 15–20% cut for new customers and keep onboarding out of the 2027 ARR plan until cohort data shows the effect.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Loss is assumed to scale linearly with the size of the increase. +12% is beyond the tested +8% (SMB) and +10% (mid-market).
Effects on new-customer win rates are not counted. That understates the cost of an SMB increase while Inkwell is pressing.
The downside case doubles every rate to cover Inkwell and renewal customers reacting more strongly than new sign-ups.
Promotion cohort reacts to price at 2× the core SMB rate (judgement).
Promotion cohort churn derived at 4.9% using mid-2026 customer counts for both halves; not reported directly.
The 2024 mid-market test covered new sign-ups, not renewals (pack uncertainty 3); existing mid-market customers may react more at renewal.
Mid-market churn rose 0.6% → 0.8% with no cause given in the pack; treated as a watch item.
How price-sensitive core SMB customers are now is unknown (pack uncertainty 1).
Whether the promotion cohort can be activated (uncertainty 2).
Trailing NRR (109.3%) assumed to repeat in 2027 and contain no price increase; each 1pt of NRR = $0.86M.
The pack has no history of new-customer ARR, so this is the key planning assumption to check.
60% of 2027 renewing enterprise ARR assumed capped at 7% (overlap not given); if all capped: −$0.2M.
Inkwell may move into deals above 200 seats, weakening mid-market pricing power.
All ARR effects are exit-2027 run-rate; recognised 2027 revenue will be lower because renewals are spread across the year.
SMB option assumes +8% on ≈2/3 of core SMB ARR from May; plan mix not given. Annual-plan customers renew once a year, so the test may need to extend to six months.
Board dashboard churn '1.4% → 2.3%' has no definition and cannot be rebuilt from segment data.
Analysis based only on the 2027 pricing briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data).
